Both analytic directions at support boundaries

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A distribution may have an analytic singularity in only one direction. A boundary of its support is more restrictive: a supporting surface forces both signs of its normal covector into the analytic wavefront. This applies to complex distributions, including smooth functions which become flat at the boundary. We prove the support theorem, extend it to limiting normals and contacts with convex open sets, and deduce uniqueness from the absence of paired directions.

Our distributions act complex-linearly, and . Write , the growth sequence of Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts. Its regular set is open; its singular set is closed in the nonzero cotangent space and conic under positive scaling. These properties and its localization and multiplication rules are proved there.

The substantive analytic input is From wavefront cones to holomorphic wedges, Theorem 7 and Corollary 8: a support boundary on the line has both analytic directions, and absence of such a pair on an interval gives uniqueness from an open zero set. Its proof uses the exact earlier holomorphic boundary and gluing theorems. Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Lemma 3 and Theorems 4 and 6, gives analytic coordinate completion, exact cotangent covariance and the projection formula. Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Theorems 2 and 5, gives proper integration and analytic-weighted integration.

Two existing programme arguments are supplied as Supporting quadratics and nearest-point normals. They are the complete geometric reductions from Sections 1 and 7 of the AN-03 lesson Curved weights and the directions in which support can end. We reuse them rather than its separate elliptic differential-equation theorem. Their calculus proofs are the metric foundation, Sections 12–13, the integral Taylor remainder in When a kernel is smooth, Section “Taylor estimates on compact neighborhoods,” and Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemmas 0.1–0.2. Tensor-test density and locality are Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B2. Fourier inversion is the Schwartz prerequisite, F1–F5; compact finite order is Order, positivity and distributional limits, Proposition 1.2. Corollary 5 (open-set uniqueness). Let be connected and open. Suppose that for no and nonzero do both and belong to . If vanishes on a nonempty open subset of , then on .

In particular the conclusion holds when for a cone with . It applies to the boundary distribution of a polynomially bounded holomorphic function on a tube with a nonempty open convex imaginary cone, whenever that boundary satisfies the forward dual-cone theorem of U075.

Proof. If were nonempty, it would be a proper relatively closed subset of . It has a relative boundary point: otherwise it would be both open and closed, disconnecting from its nonempty complement. Proposition 3 and (11) give opposite singular directions at that point, a contradiction. Thus is empty and locality gives .

A small ball inside the nonempty open cone then gives in every coordinate direction, so . The dual is therefore pointed and the boundary-distribution conclusion follows.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — smoothness does not remove the analytic normals. Put for , for , and . Determine its ordinary and analytic wavefront sets.

Solution. On , successive derivatives of are finite sums of powers of times , by the product and chain rules. Every such term tends to zero as : putting , any fixed power of is dominated by for large , as follows from the exponential series. Extending each derivative by zero therefore gives a smooth function, with every derivative zero at zero. Hence the ordinary wavefront is empty. The function is analytic off zero and has support on the line. Theorem 1 forces both analytic rays at zero, and there are no other one-dimensional nonzero directions. Exact projection covariance in U083 gives

Thus the analytic support theorem cannot be replaced by the same assertion for ordinary smooth wavefront.

Exercise 2 — why the closure is necessary. For , show that the upward covector at the origin is a supporting differential but not an exterior normal as defined by (1). Show that it is in the closure, and deduce analytic wavefront directions for the indicator distribution of .

Solution. The function is , is nonpositive on , and has differential at zero. If a witness had that differential, Taylor's formula on the boundary points would give

contradicting support from above. Away from , the same defining function is smooth and gives exterior normal at . These pairs tend to the upward covector at zero, proving the closure assertion directly. The locally integrable indicator defines a distribution of order zero. Its support is exactly : it vanishes outside, while every neighborhood of a point of meets its interior in an open set of positive measure. A nonnegative bump there has positive integral. Equation (11) now puts both vertical covectors over the origin in its analytic wavefront.

Solution. On the line the indicator of is analytic off zero. Its support boundary at zero forces both analytic directions by Theorem 1. The polynomial map is a submersion with differential . Exact analytic submersion covariance gives

Equality here uses the submersion theorem as well as the lower bound from support geometry.

Exercise 5 — every frequency direction occurs for compact support. Let have compact support in , . Show that for every nonzero there is a support point carrying both and in analytic wavefront. Explain the restriction this puts on a global conic wavefront bound.

Solution. The continuous linear function attains its maximum on the nonempty compact support. At a maximizer it satisfies (1), with differential . Theorem 1 gives both signs there. In particular the projection of to nonzero frequency directions is the whole sphere. No proper set of frequency directions, and especially no pointed cone, can contain that projection. The support point may depend on ; the statement does not put every covector over one fixed point.
